questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.syllabus_ref: 3.8 Investment appraisal (payback period, average rate of return, net present value); 3.2 Sources of finance
questions.subtopic: 3.8 Unequal asset lives, a replacement chain, and a common cost that cancels only in part

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the payback period for each machine, taking no account for now of the replacement that machine P requires at the end of year 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net present value of each machine over the four years, and state which machine should be chosen on this basis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The finance director argues that the decommissioning charge can be ignored, because both machines incur it. Justify, with a calculation, why this is only partly correct.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the value of $D$ at which the recommendation would change.

questions.challenge_mechanism: Both machines carry the same decommissioning charge, so the obvious move is to cancel it and compare the rest. But the two machines do not decommission at the same time: one pays the charge twice over the four-year horizon and the other pays it once. The payment at the end of year four is genuinely common and does cancel; the payment at the end of year two is not, and it is the single term that decides the whole question. Cancelling both removes exactly the term that carries the decision.
questions.question:
Vastra Teknik must choose between two machines for a four-year contract. The contract will
generate net cash inflows of $\pounds 90{,}000$ a year for each of the four years whichever machine
is used, so the choice turns entirely on the costs. The company's cost of capital is $10\%$ per
year and all cash flows arise at the ends of years.

**Machine P** costs $\pounds 120{,}000$ and has a working life of two years, so it must be replaced
by an identical machine at the end of year 2 at the same price. It is decommissioned at the end of
year 2 and again at the end of year 4.

**Machine Q** costs $\pounds 230{,}000$ and has a working life of four years, so it is not replaced.
It is decommissioned once, at the end of year 4.

The decommissioning charge is $\pounds D$ on each occasion it arises, and is the same for both
machines. Assume initially that $D = 20{,}000$.

(a) Calculate the payback period for each machine. \tag{3}

(b) Calculate the net present value of each machine over the four years, and state which machine
should be chosen on this basis. \tag{5}

(c) The finance director argues that the decommissioning charge can be ignored, because both
machines incur it and it will therefore cancel. Explain, with a calculation, why this is only
partly correct. \tag{4}

(d) Determine the value of $D$ at which the recommendation would change. \tag{4}
questions.answer:
(a) Machine P returns $\pounds 90{,}000$ a year against an outlay of $\pounds 120{,}000$, so

$$\text{payback}_{P} = \frac{120{,}000}{90{,}000} = 1.33 \text{ years}$$

which is about one year and four months (A1). Machine Q recovers $\pounds 230{,}000$ at the same
rate, so

$$\text{payback}_{Q} = \frac{230{,}000}{90{,}000} = 2.56 \text{ years}$$

or roughly two years and seven months (A1). On payback, P is the clear winner, recovering its cost
more than a year sooner (A1). Note that payback ignores the second purchase P must make at the end
of year 2, which is one reason the ranking it produces should not be trusted on its own.

(b) The four-year annuity factor at $10\%$ is

$$\frac{1}{1.1} + \frac{1}{1.1^{2}} + \frac{1}{1.1^{3}} + \frac{1}{1.1^{4}} = 3.1699$$

so the present value of the inflows, identical for both machines, is

$$90{,}000 \times 3.1699 = \pounds 285{,}288 \tag{A1}$$

For P the outflows are the purchase at $t = 0$, the replacement at $t = 2$, and decommissioning at
$t = 2$ and $t = 4$ (M1):

$$120{,}000 + \frac{120{,}000}{1.1^{2}} + \frac{20{,}000}{1.1^{2}} + \frac{20{,}000}{1.1^{4}}
= 120{,}000 + 99{,}174 + 16{,}529 + 13{,}660 = \pounds 249{,}363 \tag{A1}$$

For Q the outflows are the single purchase at $t = 0$ and decommissioning at $t = 4$ (M1):

$$230{,}000 + \frac{20{,}000}{1.1^{4}} = 230{,}000 + 13{,}660 = \pounds 243{,}660 \tag{A1}$$

Hence

$$\text{NPV}_{P} = 285{,}288 - 249{,}363 = \pounds 35{,}925, \qquad
\text{NPV}_{Q} = 285{,}288 - 243{,}660 = \pounds 41{,}628 \tag{A1}$$

Both are positive, so both are worth undertaking; on net present value **Q should be chosen**, by
$\pounds 5{,}702$ (A1). This reverses the payback ranking in (a), and it also reverses the average
rate of return, which favours P at $16.7\%$ against $12.0\%$ for Q precisely because P is measured
against a much smaller capital base.

(c) The director is right about one of the two payments and wrong about the other. Both machines
pay $D$ at the end of year 4, and that payment is multiplied by the same discount factor
$\frac{1}{1.1^{4}}$ in both columns, so it is common and does cancel (A1). Machine P, however, also
pays $D$ at the end of year 2, and Q pays nothing at that date; this payment has no counterpart to
cancel against (A1). Its present value is

$$\frac{20{,}000}{1.1^{2}} = \pounds 16{,}529 \tag{A1}$$

so the decommissioning charge contributes $\pounds 16{,}529$ to the difference between the two
machines — not zero, and not the $\pounds 33{,}058$ that a candidate who doubled it would report. The
claim is therefore only partly correct: the charge is irrelevant to the comparison in year 4 and
decisive in year 2 (A1).

The practical consequence is that the charge is not a detail. Without it the two machines would
differ by

$$(120{,}000 + 99{,}174) - 230{,}000 = -\pounds 10{,}826$$

in P's favour, and P would be chosen. It is the year-2 payment alone, worth $\pounds 16{,}529$, that
overturns a gap of $\pounds 10{,}826$ and turns the decision round.

(d) Let the decommissioning charge be $D$. The year-4 payments cancel as before, so the difference
between the present values of the two cost streams is

$$\left(120{,}000 + \frac{120{,}000}{1.1^{2}} + \frac{D}{1.1^{2}} + \frac{D}{1.1^{4}}\right)
- \left(230{,}000 + \frac{D}{1.1^{4}}\right) = -10{,}826 + \frac{D}{1.1^{2}} \tag{M1}$$

where the two $\frac{D}{1.1^{4}}$ terms have been cancelled (A1). Q is preferred while this is
positive and P while it is negative, so the recommendation changes where

$$-10{,}826 + \frac{D}{1.21} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad D = 10{,}826 \times 1.21
= \pounds 13{,}100 \tag{A1}$$

At $D = 13{,}100$ the two machines are exactly equivalent, and the firm is indifferent (A1). Since
the actual charge of $\pounds 20{,}000$ exceeds $\pounds 13{,}100$, Q is confirmed as the better
choice — but the margin is $\pounds 5{,}702$, and a decommissioning quote that came in under
$\pounds 13{,}100$ would switch the decision to P.
questions.markscheme_notes: (a) One mark for each payback figure, one for the comparison. Accept 1.3 and 2.6 years or the equivalent in months. Allow follow-through to (b) from a payback error. (b) One mark for the present value of the inflows, one for identifying the four outflow terms for P, one for the P total, one for the Q total, one for the two NPVs and the recommendation. Do not award the recommendation mark without both NPVs. Condone rounding to the nearest pound throughout; the exact totals are 249,362.75 and 243,660.27. A candidate who omits the replacement purchase should lose the term mark but may still earn the method mark for discounting. (c) One mark for saying the year-4 payment cancels, one for saying the year-2 payment does not, one for the figure 16,529, one for the conclusion that the claim is partly right. Credit the figure even if the candidate describes it as 'the extra cost of P'. (d) One mark for setting up the difference with the year-4 terms cancelled, one for the equation, one for D = 13,100, one for stating which machine wins on either side of it. A candidate who cancels both D terms gets -10,826 and should be held at the first mark: the point of the part is precisely that the cancellation is only partial.
questions.explanation:
This item turns on a piece of arithmetic that looks like bookkeeping and is in fact the
whole decision. Two identical charges are described in the same words, and the instinct is to treat
them the same way. They are not the same: one occurs at a date when both machines are spending money
and the other at a date when only one is. Discounting preserves that difference, nominal addition
destroys it, and the item is built so that the destroyed difference is larger than the gap it
overturns.

The naive path is to take the finance director at his word. If both decommissioning payments are
dropped, P costs $120{,}000 + 99{,}174 = \pounds 219{,}174$ against Q's $\pounds 230{,}000$, P wins
by $\pounds 10{,}826$, and no value of $D$ can change that — the answer to part (d) becomes 'the
charge makes no difference'. That is a confident, well-argued, entirely wrong answer, and it is
wrong because of one omission rather than one mistake. Nothing in the stem says the two payments
happen at different times; the candidate has to read the replacement chain and notice it.

What makes the item worth sixteen marks rather than six is that the correct treatment then has to be
carried through three different appraisal methods that disagree with each other. Payback favours P
by more than a year. Average rate of return favours P by nearly five percentage points, for the
reason that P is measured against a smaller capital base and is therefore flattered by any
percentage measure. Net present value favours Q, because it is the only one of the three that sees
the second purchase at the end of year 2 and the second decommissioning charge that comes with it.
A candidate who reports all three rankings and then recommends Q on the grounds that NPV accounts
for the timing of every cash flow over the full horizon has done the real work; a candidate who
reports one ranking and stops has not, however accurate the arithmetic.

The item is adapted from a UK A-Level investment-appraisal question that asks which of two machines
to buy given their purchase prices and running costs. The replacement chain, the decommissioning
charge, the partial cancellation and the break-even value of $D$ are all new here. The source asks
for a decision; this asks for the decision, for the term that produces it, and for the parameter
value at which it flips. That last move is what forces the cancellation to be understood rather than
performed, and it is why the item sits at difficulty 4 rather than 3.

provenance.inspired_by: UK A-Level Business investment appraisal: choose between two machines with different purchase prices and running costs
provenance.resource_origin: UK A-Level Business / Economics investment appraisal data-response questions
provenance.adaptation: The source archetype supplies two machines, two prices and a stream of running costs, and asks which to buy. Here the running costs are made identical so they cancel and the entire decision moves to the capital and decommissioning terms; a two-year life against a four-year life introduces a replacement chain; a common decommissioning charge is attached so that one occurrence cancels and one does not; and the final part asks for the parameter value at which the recommendation flips, which has no counterpart in the source. Context, structure, given-versus-asked and reasoning chain are all changed.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Treat the decommissioning charge as common and cancel both occurrences, giving P a cost advantage of 10,826 that no value of D can alter, and answer (d) with 'the charge is irrelevant'.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: Machine P is replaced at the end of year 2, so it decommissions twice over the four-year horizon while Q decommissions once. Only the year-4 charge is common; the year-2 charge, worth 16,529 in present value, has no counterpart and is larger than the 10,826 gap it overturns.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: Choose P, with the reasoning that identical charges cancel. This is reached by a candidate who discounts correctly, sets up both columns correctly, and then removes the one term that decides the question.

verification.method: Every discounted figure recomputed from the stated cash flows; the cancellation checked by differencing the two present-value expressions symbolically so that only the 1/1.1^4 terms disappear; the break-even D solved and then substituted back to confirm the two present values agree to the penny.
solution_skeleton: discount the four identical inflows to establish the common revenue term
list the outflow terms for each machine, including the replacement purchase
identify which decommissioning payment is common and which is not
difference the two present values with only the common term cancelled
solve the resulting linear equation in D for the switch-over value

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.syllabus_ref: 5.5 Break-even analysis (contribution, break-even output, margin of safety, profit targets); 3.3 Costs and revenues
questions.subtopic: 5.5 Break-even with a stepped fixed cost: two break-even points and a region of loss above the first

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even output on the assumption that fixed costs remain at $60{,}000$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that profit at an output of $8{,}000$ units is $4{,}000$, while profit at an output of $8{,}001$ units is $-20{,}992$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the output at which the business breaks even for the second time.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate whether the business should plan an output of $10{,}000$ units, supporting your answer with a calculation of the minimum selling price required.

questions.challenge_mechanism: Break-even is taught as one number, and the formula is applied without asking whether the fixed cost is actually fixed over the range being examined. Here it is not: above $8{,}000$ units a second shift is needed and fixed costs step up by $\pounds 25{,}000$. The single figure the formula gives, $7{,}500$ units, is a valid break-even point and a dangerously incomplete answer, because profit is positive at $8{,}000$ units, negative at $8{,}001$, and does not recover until $10{,}625$. There are two break-even points and a loss-making region between them.
questions.answer:
(a) Contribution per unit is

$$\pounds 14 - \pounds 6 = \pounds 8 \tag{A1}$$

and break-even output is fixed cost divided by contribution per unit (M1):

$$\frac{60{,}000}{8} = 7{,}500 \text{ units} \tag{A1}$$

This lies below $8{,}000$ units, so the $\pounds 60{,}000$ figure is the right one to use and the
answer is consistent.

(b) At $8{,}000$ units the higher fixed cost has not yet been triggered, so

$$\text{profit} = 8 \times 8{,}000 - 60{,}000 = 64{,}000 - 60{,}000 = \pounds 4{,}000 \tag{M1A1}$$

At $8{,}001$ units the step applies to the whole year's output, so fixed costs are
$\pounds 85{,}000$ and not $\pounds 60{,}000$ (M1):

$$\text{profit} = 8 \times 8{,}001 - 85{,}000 = 64{,}008 - 85{,}000 = -\pounds 20{,}992 \tag{A1}$$

The two figures differ by $\pounds 24{,}992$ even though output has risen by a single unit (A1). Of
that, $\pounds 8$ is the contribution earned by the extra unit and $\pounds 25{,}000$ is the step in
fixed cost, so almost the entire movement is the step and not the unit. A profit-and-loss account
drawn up for any output from $8{,}001$ units upwards must therefore use $\pounds 85{,}000$, and the
$7{,}500$-unit figure from (a) tells the business nothing about that region.

(c) In the upper band, fixed costs are $\pounds 85{,}000$ and contribution per unit is unchanged at
$\pounds 8$ (M1):

$$\frac{85{,}000}{8} = 10{,}625 \text{ units} \tag{A1}$$

At $10{,}625$ units contribution is $8 \times 10{,}625 = \pounds 85{,}000$, which exactly covers the
higher fixed cost, so profit is zero (A1). Because $10{,}625 > 8{,}000$ the answer lies inside the
band to which it applies and is self-consistent, exactly as in (a) (A1).

The business therefore breaks even twice, at $7{,}500$ units and again at $10{,}625$ units, and
makes a loss at every output in between, with the single worst point being $8{,}001$ units. Any
output from $10{,}626$ units upward is profitable. The margin of safety at a planned output of
$12{,}000$ units is $12{,}000 - 10{,}625 = 1{,}375$ units, or $11.5\%$ — measured against the second
break-even point, not the first, which would give a meaningless $37.5\%$.

(d) At $10{,}000$ units the business is in the upper band, so fixed costs are $\pounds 85{,}000$
(M1). Let the selling price be $p$; contribution per unit is $p - 6$ (M1). Break-even requires

$$10{,}000(p - 6) = 85{,}000 \tag{A1}$$

so

$$p = \frac{85{,}000}{10{,}000} + 6 = 8.50 + 6 = \pounds 14.50 \tag{A1}$$

The current price of $\pounds 14.00$ gives a contribution of $\pounds 80{,}000$ against fixed costs
of $\pounds 85{,}000$ and a loss of $\pounds 5{,}000$, so the required increase is $\pounds 0.50$,
or $3.6\%$. Two cautions are worth recording. The answer is the break-even price at this output, not
a recommended price: at $\pounds 14.50$ the business makes exactly nothing on $10{,}000$ units, and a
price below $\pounds 14.50$ loses money. And the answer is specific to $10{,}000$ units, because the
$\pounds 85{,}000$ is spread over whatever volume is actually produced; at $12{,}000$ units the
break-even price would be only $\pounds 13.08$.
questions.markscheme_notes: (a) One mark for the contribution, one for dividing fixed cost by contribution, one for the figure 7,500. Award the final mark only if the candidate states or implies that 7,500 is below 8,000 and therefore consistent. (b) One mark for using 60,000 at 8,000 units, one for the 4,000, one for switching to 85,000 at 8,001 units, one for the -20,992, one for noting that the whole step and not just the extra unit drives the change. A candidate who applies 85,000 to only the units above 8,000 gets 3,992 and should lose the third and fourth marks. (c) One mark for using 85,000, one for dividing by 8, one for 10,625, one for checking that the answer lies in the band to which it applies. Allow 10,625 or 10,626; do not allow 7,500 as the only answer. (d) One mark for using 85,000 rather than 60,000, one for setting up the equation, one for 14.50, one for the interpretation. Accept a correctly argued answer in pence. Follow-through applies throughout: a candidate who misreads the step but is otherwise consistent should not be penalised twice.
questions.explanation:
Break-even analysis is one of the first quantitative tools a business student meets, and
it is normally taught as the answer to a single question: how many units must we sell? The formula
is short enough to memorise, and the memorised version carries an assumption that is almost never
examined — that the fixed cost stays fixed across the range of output being considered. Here it does
not, and the item is built so that the assumption fails exactly where a manager would most want to
rely on it.

The naive path is to compute contribution, divide, and stop: $60{,}000$ over $8$ gives $7{,}500$
units, the business plans to sell well above that, and everything looks sound. That answer is not
wrong as far as it goes, and it is self-consistent, which is what makes it dangerous. It says
nothing at all about the region above $8{,}000$ units, and in that region the same formula applied to
the same cost structure gives a loss of nearly $\pounds 21{,}000$. A manager acting on the first
number would expand output into the step and be worse off than before expanding, having been told by
the arithmetic that the expansion was safe.

The discontinuity is worth dwelling on, because it is the point that separates understanding the
formula from being able to use it. Profit at $8{,}000$ units is $\pounds 4{,}000$; at $8{,}001$ it is
$-\pounds 20{,}992$. One extra unit destroys nearly $\pounds 25{,}000$ of profit, of which
$\pounds 8$ comes from the unit and the remaining $\pounds 25{,}000$ from the step. A candidate who
writes that down has understood that the step applies to the year's whole output rather than to the
marginal units, which is the single idea the item exists to test, and which the phrase "applies to
the whole year's output" in the stem is there to make decidable rather than ambiguous.

Two further moves carry the item past routine application. Part (c) asks for the second break-even
point and requires the candidate to check that the answer lies inside the band to which it applies
— the same consistency check that part (a) demanded, but now on the far side of the step, where the
obvious answer and the correct answer are different numbers. Part (d) then inverts the question,
fixing output and solving for price, which is the version a manager actually faces and which exposes
anyone who has been applying the formula mechanically: using $\pounds 60{,}000$ instead of
$\pounds 85{,}000$ here gives $\pounds 12.00$ and understates the required price by two pounds.

The item is adapted from a UK A-Level treatment of break-even that introduces a stepped fixed cost
and asks for the revised chart. Asking for the two break-even points explicitly, demanding the
profit figures on either side of the step so that the discontinuity has to be stated as a number,
and inverting to solve for price rather than for output are all new here. The source wants a
picture; this wants the candidate to locate a region of loss that a correctly drawn chart would show
but a single calculated figure would hide.

provenance.inspired_by: UK A-Level Business break-even with a stepped (semi-variable) fixed cost and a revised break-even chart
provenance.resource_origin: UK A-Level Business / Economics break-even questions with stepped fixed costs
provenance.adaptation: The source archetype gives a cost that steps at a stated output and asks for a revised chart or a single new break-even figure. Here the step is large enough that profit is positive immediately below it and strongly negative immediately above it, producing two break-even points with a loss-making region between them; parts (b) and (c) force that region to be stated numerically rather than drawn; and part (d) inverts the relation to solve for price at a fixed output. Context, structure, given-versus-asked and reasoning chain are all changed.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Compute contribution as 8, divide 60,000 by 8, report 7,500 units as the break-even output, and treat every output above it as profitable.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: Fixed costs are 60,000 only up to 8,000 units. Above that output they step to 85,000 for the whole year, so profit falls from +4,000 at 8,000 units to -20,992 at 8,001 and does not return to zero until 10,625 units.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: A single break-even output of 7,500 units, with the conclusion that any output above it is profitable. At the planned output of 10,000 units this reports a profit of 20,000 when the true result is a loss of 5,000.

verification.method: Profit recomputed from first principles at 8,000 and 8,001 units with the appropriate fixed cost in each case; the second break-even point checked by substitution to confirm that contribution exactly equals the higher fixed cost; the break-even price substituted back to confirm that 10,000 units at 14.50 gives zero profit.
solution_skeleton: compute contribution per unit from price and variable cost
apply the lower fixed cost to find the first break-even output
switch to the higher fixed cost above 8,000 units and evaluate profit either side of the step
divide the higher fixed cost by contribution for the second break-even output
invert the relation to solve for the break-even price at a fixed output

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.syllabus_ref: 2.1 Introduction to human resource management (workforce planning, labour turnover, absenteeism); 6.7 Descriptive statistics
questions.subtopic: 2.1 Labour turnover as a weighted aggregate: recovering a missing department and targeting the right one

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of staff who left department B during the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the labour turnover rate for each department and confirm the overall rate of $14.4$ per cent.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the overall rate is not the average of the three departmental rates, and explain why the difference arises.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The human resources director proposes an overall target of $10$ per cent and must choose between reducing department A turnover to $5$ per cent and reducing department C turnover to $10$ per cent. Evaluate which should be prioritised.

questions.challenge_mechanism: Three departments report turnover, and the overall rate is not the average of them. It is a headcount-weighted aggregate, and the weighting is what carries every conclusion in the item. The smallest department has the highest rate and the second-smallest has the second-highest, so the department a manager would target on the rates alone is the one that contributes least to the headline figure. Cutting the largest department from $7.5\%$ to $5\%$ moves the overall rate by $1.2$ points; cutting the smallest from $22\%$ to $10\%$ moves it by $2.4$ — twice as much, from $42\%$ of the headcount.
questions.question:
Haldane Logistics employs $250$ staff in three departments. The workforce plan records
the number of staff who left during the year, but the entry for department B has been lost.

| Department | Number employed | Number leaving during the year |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 120 | 9 |
| B | 80 | not recorded |
| C | 50 | 11 |

The company's overall labour turnover for the year is known to have been $14.4\%$. Each leaver
costs the business $\pounds 3{,}500$ to replace, covering recruitment, training and lost output.

Labour turnover is calculated as

$$\text{labour turnover} = \frac{\text{number of staff leaving during the year}}
{\text{number of staff employed}} \times 100.$$

(a) Calculate the number of staff who left department B during the year. \tag{3}

(b) Calculate the labour turnover rate for each department and confirm the overall rate of
$14.4\%$. \tag{5}

(c) Show that the overall rate is not the average of the three departmental rates, and explain why
the difference arises. \tag{4}

(d) The human resources director proposes an overall target of $10\%$ and must choose between two
interventions: reducing department A's turnover to $5\%$, or reducing department C's turnover to
$10\%$. Evaluate which should be prioritised. \tag{4}
questions.answer:
(a) Overall turnover of $14.4\%$ on $250$ staff gives a total of

$$0.144 \times 250 = 36 \text{ leavers} \tag{M1}$$

of which $9$ came from A and $11$ from C, so department B accounts for (M1)

$$36 - 9 - 11 = 16 \text{ leavers} \tag{A1}$$

(b) Applying the formula to each department in turn (M1):

$$\text{A}: \frac{9}{120} \times 100 = 7.5\%, \qquad
\text{B}: \frac{16}{80} \times 100 = 20.0\%, \qquad
\text{C}: \frac{11}{50} \times 100 = 22.0\% \tag{A1A1A1}$$

The overall rate is the total leaving divided by the total employed, not the average of the three
percentages:

$$\frac{9 + 16 + 11}{120 + 80 + 50} \times 100 = \frac{36}{250} \times 100 = 14.4\% \tag{M1A1}$$

which confirms the figure given.

(c) The simple average of the three departmental rates is

$$\frac{7.5 + 20.0 + 22.0}{3} = \frac{49.5}{3} = 16.5\% \tag{M1A1}$$

against a true overall rate of $14.4\%$, so the average overstates turnover by $2.1$ percentage
points (A1). The reason is that the departments are not the same size. The average gives each
department's rate a weight of one third, but department A actually employs $48\%$ of the workforce
and department C only $20\%$ (A1). The overall rate is a weighted mean in which each department's
rate is weighted by its headcount:

$$\frac{120(7.5) + 80(20.0) + 50(22.0)}{250}
= \frac{900 + 1{,}600 + 1{,}100}{250} = \frac{3{,}600}{250} = 14.4\%$$

The $7.5\%$ earned by the largest department pulls the figure down more than the $22\%$ earned by
the smallest pulls it up, which is exactly the effect the unweighted average discards.

(d) Reducing department A to $5\%$ means $0.05 \times 120 = 6$ leavers, a saving of $3$ (M1). Total
leavers fall to $33$ and the overall rate becomes

$$\frac{33}{250} \times 100 = 13.2\% \tag{A1}$$

an improvement of $1.2$ percentage points, at a saving of $3 \times 3{,}500 = \pounds 10{,}500$.

Reducing department C to $10\%$ means $0.10 \times 50 = 5$ leavers, a saving of $6$ (M1). Total
leavers fall to $30$ and the overall rate becomes

$$\frac{30}{250} \times 100 = 12.0\% \tag{A1}$$

an improvement of $2.4$ percentage points, at a saving of $6 \times 3{,}500 = \pounds 21{,}000$.

Department C should be prioritised. It delivers twice the reduction in the overall rate and twice
the cost saving, from $20\%$ of the workforce rather than $48\%$ (A1). The reason is that the
improvement depends on two things multiplied together — the size of the department and the size of
the cut — and department C's cut is $12$ percentage points against department A's $2.5$.

Two qualifications belong in a full answer. Neither intervention reaches the $10\%$ target on its
own: both together give $12.0\%$, and hitting $10\%$ would require $25$ leavers in total, so a
further five must come from somewhere. And the arithmetic is silent on why people leave. Department
C's $22\%$ may reflect working conditions, pay or management, and if the underlying cause is not
addressed the reduction may prove temporary; conversely, if department A's low turnover reflects a
genuinely well-managed operation, cutting it further may be the cheapest of all. The numbers say
where the leverage is, not what to do about it (A1).
questions.markscheme_notes: (a) One mark for converting 14.4% of 250 to 36 leavers, one for subtracting the known leavers, one for the figure 16. (b) One mark for applying the formula, one for each of the three departmental rates, one for dividing total leavers by total employed. Do not award a rate calculated as an average of the others. Accept rates to one decimal place. (c) One mark for the average of 16.5%, one for the comparison with 14.4%, one for explaining that the departments differ in size, one for the weighted-mean calculation or an equivalent explanation in words. A candidate who says only 'the average is wrong' without saying why should be held at two marks. (d) One mark for the 3 leavers saved in A, one for 13.2%, one for the 6 leavers saved in C, one for 12.0%. The evaluation mark is awarded for a supported choice of C; allow A only if a cost or feasibility argument is given. Credit the 10,500 and 21,000 figures even if the candidate backs the other option. Follow-through: a candidate who finds 16 in (a) by a different route should not be penalised again in (b), provided the method is consistent.
questions.explanation:
Labour turnover is a ratio, and ratios built from parts do not behave like the parts.
Every student knows this in principle and almost nobody applies it under pressure, because the
unweighted average is quicker to compute and feels like a fair summary. This item makes the shortcut
cost something: the average gives $16.5\%$ against a true $14.4\%$, and a manager working from the
higher figure would set targets against a rate the business never had.

The naive path in part (d) is to read the three rates, see that department C is worst at $22\%$, and
then notice that department A is four times its size and conclude that A must be where the numbers
are. That is a plausible argument and it is wrong, because the gain from an intervention is the
product of two quantities rather than either one alone. Department A offers a cut of $2.5$
percentage points on $120$ staff, worth three leavers. Department C offers a cut of $12$ points on
$50$ staff, worth six. The smaller department wins by a factor of two, and it wins on cost as well
as on the headline rate, because the replacement cost attaches to leavers rather than to
percentages.

Part (a) is doing more work than it appears to. Recovering a missing component of an aggregate is
not a routine operation in a business context, and it forces the candidate to hold the aggregate and
its parts in mind at the same time — which is precisely the mental posture the rest of the item
needs. It also makes the weighted structure unavoidable in part (b), because the three departmental
rates have to reconcile with a total that was supplied before any of them was known.

The final part asks for an evaluation rather than a calculation, which is deliberate. The arithmetic
points one way and it points clearly, but it rests on an assumption — that turnover can be reduced by
a stated number of points in a chosen department — that the data does nothing to support. A candidate
who recommends C, gives the figures, and then observes that the cause of C's turnover is unknown and
that neither intervention reaches the target has done the whole question. One who produces only
$12.0\%$ and $13.2\%$ has done the arithmetic and stopped, and that is the difference between a
business answer and a numeracy answer.

The item is adapted from a UK A-Level human-resource data-response that supplies a table of
departmental turnover and asks which department the business should be most concerned about. Making
one entry missing so that the aggregate has to be recovered, making the smallest department the
highest-turnover one so that the rates and the contributions point in opposite directions, and
requiring the two interventions to be compared in both percentage and money terms are all new here.
The source asks for an identification; this asks for a decision that the identification would get
wrong.

provenance.inspired_by: UK A-Level Business human resource data-response: departmental labour turnover table and a judgement about which department matters most
provenance.resource_origin: UK A-Level Business / Economics HR data-response questions on labour turnover
provenance.adaptation: The source archetype supplies a complete table and asks the candidate to identify the department of greatest concern, which the highest rate answers directly. Here one entry is deleted so the missing component must be recovered from the known aggregate before any rate can be computed; the department sizes are arranged so that the highest rate belongs to the smallest department, making the rate ranking and the contribution ranking point in opposite directions; and the final part requires two named interventions to be compared in both percentage and monetary terms and then evaluated rather than identified. Context, structure, given-versus-asked and reasoning chain are all changed.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Read the three departmental rates, note that C is highest at 22%, and conclude either that C should be targeted because it is worst or that A should be targeted because it is largest — treating the overall rate as the average of the three.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The overall rate is a headcount-weighted aggregate, not an average; A carries 48% of the workforce and C only 20%. The gain from an intervention is the product of department size and the size of the cut, so C's 12-point cut on 50 staff saves 6 leavers against A's 2.5-point cut on 120 staff saving 3.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: Target department A, on the grounds that it employs 48% of the workforce, giving an overall rate of 13.2% and a saving of 10,500 — half the improvement and half the saving of the alternative, and a recommendation that leaves the worst-performing department untouched.

verification.method: The missing component recovered from the aggregate and checked by re-adding the three departments; every rate recomputed from the raw counts; the weighted mean shown to equal the unweighted total divided by total employed; both interventions substituted back to confirm the resulting overall rates.
solution_skeleton: convert the known overall rate into a total number of leavers
subtract the recorded departments to recover the missing one
compute each departmental rate and reconcile them with the overall rate
compare the unweighted average with the headcount-weighted aggregate
evaluate both interventions in leavers saved, percentage points and cost
